questions.q: What real-world problem does this lesson exist to prevent?
options: Two tools each getting their own separate data extract and computing a business rule like scrap rate slightly differently, so their reports quietly disagree
SSRS and Power BI being unable to connect to SQL Server at all
The SSIS package running twice per night instead of once
dw.FactWorkOrder having too many columns for either tool to read
questions.explain: Giving each tool its own copy or its own version of a business rule is exactly how two 'correct' reports end up disagreeing with each other — the single most common way a BI team loses trust in its numbers.

questions.q: How does WorkOrderProductionSummary.rdl connect to the warehouse?
options: Through a shared data source — a connection definition stored once and referenced by any report that needs it
Through a connection string embedded directly and uniquely inside that one report only
It does not connect to the warehouse at all; it reads a flat file export
Through the same Power Query engine Power BI uses
questions.explain: A shared data source is reused across reports, so a second report added later points at the same connection rather than duplicating it.

questions.q: Which of these is true about how SSRS and Power BI connect to the warehouse in this project?
options: They use two different connection mechanisms, but point at the exact same server, database, schema, and tables
They must use the identical connection mechanism, or the numbers will never match
Power BI connects to the warehouse only through SSRS, never directly
SSRS and Power BI cannot both connect to the same SQL Server database
questions.explain: A shared data source (SSRS) and a Power Query SQL Server connection (Power BI) are different mechanisms, but this lesson's whole point is that they resolve to the identical warehouse tables.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what should happen if the SSRS report's scrap rate and the Power BI dashboard's scrap rate for the same product don't match?
options: Look for a filter, date range, or rounding difference between the two expressions — the bug is almost never in either report itself
Assume Power BI's number is always correct and change the SSRS report to match it without investigating
Rebuild the entire warehouse from scratch immediately
Ignore the discrepancy, since some disagreement between tools is expected
questions.explain: If both tools genuinely read the same warehouse tables, a mismatch almost always traces back to a difference in filtering, date range, or rounding between the two expressions, not the warehouse itself.

questions.q: Why does getting the warehouse's grain, keys, and column definitions right in Lessons 5-6 matter so much to this lesson?
options: Every downstream tool inherits that correctness (or that error) for free, since both SSRS and Power BI read directly from the warehouse without redefining anything themselves
The warehouse's grain has no effect on either SSRS or Power BI
SSRS and Power BI each apply their own grain on top of the warehouse's, overriding it
Grain only matters for Power BI, not for SSRS reports
questions.explain: Because neither tool redefines the warehouse's grain or keys, whatever is correct — or wrong — in dw.FactWorkOrder passes straight through to every report built on it.
